newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK --Quiet, dataless session seen.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK --Quiet, dataless session seen.

text.p: A light day of trading was expected in U.S. government securities on Friday, with no economic data releases to give players direction.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan will speak on regulatory matters and Fed Vice Chairwoman Alice Rivlin will moderate a panel at the Atlanta Fed's conference. Kansas City Fed president Thomas Hoenig will speak at 1030 EST/1530 GMT.
Some market participants expressed concern that U.S. dollar weakening would carry overnight from Thursday and depress Treasuries prices in Tokyo.

"You could make a case that we're going to see a quiet session Friday as there's nothing scheduled and the market still has the upcoming challenge of Chairman Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkings testimony to get through. Wednesday is the first day and the first days are usually the ones that generate the most static," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

Supply also becomes a concern next week with two- and five-year note auctions and regular weekly bills, Flanagan said, another reason trading activity was likely to be lightly traded in thin ranges on Friday.

Flanagan noted that Greenspan was scheduled to speak on bank regulatory topics and few expected any comments on the economy. Nevertheless, Greenspan's remarks would be closely monitored as "he just might provide the catalyst the market needs to get going one way or the other," he said.
"The market may be a little bit defensive after a really good run. We've rallied about 40 basis points since the end of January," said Stuart Hoffman, senior economist at PNC Financial Corp.
Bond market yields remained at the lower end of the recent trading range, so yields may be going higher, he said.
But Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp., wasn't one of them.
"That's a misperception. Any foreign selling wouldn't affect the market for more than a couple of hours," Platt said.

Instead, the market was keyed on Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkings testimony before Congress February 26 and 27 and the National Association of Purchasing Management and employment reports the week following, Platt said.

"The economic data for Janaury and February seem to have a little bit of a stronger feel to them, particularly on the buy side of the economy," Hoffman said. "Gold has bounced back with some of the other basic industrial commodities."
Hoffman said the dollar seemed to be settling instead of gaining more strength.
"When the market couldn't rally in the face of Wednesday's very good consumer price report, it had to tell you that the market is really just tired at this point, Hoffman said.
CPI rose only 0.1 percent in both the overall and core rates and followed a fall in producer prices the prior week.

"We broke through some crucial levels Thursday and some people had set up shorts and may not want to hold them over the weekend," said Jerry Zukowski, economist at PaineWebber Inc. "But it's hard to see whether the lower levels would be validated as futures were already closed Thursday."
"But there is no reason to push the market in one direction or the other," Zukowski said.
